objectives: Explain how digital hearing aids use wide-dynamic-range compression and feedback cancellation.
Describe the cochlear implant: electrode array, place coding, and processing strategies.
Distinguish bone-anchored devices and match each technology to the appropriate hearing loss.

slides.title: Digital hearing aids
slides.body:
A modern **hearing aid** is not a simple amplifier; it is a wearable **digital signal processing (DSP)** computer that reshapes sound to fit a damaged cochlea. Every aid has the same signal chain: a **microphone** (often two or more, for directionality) converts sound to an electrical signal, an analog-to-digital converter samples it, a DSP chip processes it, and a tiny loudspeaker called the **receiver** delivers the result to the ear. Styles range from **behind-the-ear (BTE)** and **receiver-in-canal (RIC)** to **in-the-ear (ITE)** and nearly invisible **completely-in-canal (CIC)** designs, chosen by hearing loss, dexterity, and cosmetics.

The central processing problem is the **mismatch between dynamic ranges**. A normal ear handles a roughly **120 dB** range from threshold to discomfort, but a person with sensorineural loss often has **elevated thresholds** (soft sounds inaudible) yet a **normal or even lowered discomfort level** (loud sounds still loud), thanks to loudness **recruitment** from outer-hair-cell damage. Their usable **residual dynamic range** may be only **30-40 dB**. The solution is **wide-dynamic-range compression (WDRC)**: the aid applies **high gain to soft sounds** and **little or no gain to loud sounds**, compressing the wide acoustic world into the patient's narrow comfortable window. The amount of gain at each input level and in each frequency band is set during a **prescriptive fitting** using validated formulas such as **NAL-NL2** (from Australia's **National Acoustic Laboratories**) or **DSL v5** (the **Desired Sensation Level** method from Western University in Canada), with a probe microphone in the canal performing **real-ear measurement** to verify the actual output at the eardrum matches the target.

DSP enables features impossible in old analog aids. **Multichannel processing** splits the signal into many frequency bands so gain and compression can be tuned to the exact shape of the audiogram. **Adaptive directional microphones** form beams toward the front to suppress noise from behind. **Digital noise reduction** estimates the noise floor in each band and trims steady-state noise. **Frequency lowering** (frequency compression or transposition) shifts inaudible high-frequency energy down into a region the patient can still hear. And **feedback cancellation** tackles the squeal that occurs when amplified sound leaks back from the receiver into the microphone and re-amplifies in a loop: the DSP runs an **adaptive filter** that continuously models the feedback path and subtracts a predicted copy of the leaked signal before it can build up, allowing much higher stable gain than analog aids ever achieved. Modern aids add **Bluetooth** streaming, rechargeable batteries, telecoils for hearing loops, and even onboard machine-learning scene classifiers, but the core mission is unchanged: make speech audible and comfortable across a damaged dynamic range.

slides.title: The cochlear implant
slides.body:
When hair-cell loss is so severe that no amount of acoustic amplification helps, hearing can be restored by **bypassing the dead cochlea entirely** and stimulating the **auditory nerve** with electricity. This is the **cochlear implant (CI)**, arguably the most successful neural prosthesis ever built and the first to substantially restore a human sense. Its development is associated with **William House**, an American otologist who implanted single-channel devices from the 1960s and 1970s, and especially **Graeme Clark** in Australia, whose team at the University of Melbourne developed the **multichannel** implant in the late 1970s that became the foundation of modern devices (commercialized by Cochlear Ltd. as the Nucleus). Other pioneers include the team at the **University of California, San Francisco** and **Blake Wilson**, whose processing strategies (below) dramatically improved speech understanding.

A cochlear implant has an **external** part and an **internal** part. Externally, a **microphone** and **speech processor** capture and analyze sound, and a **transmitter coil** held on the scalp by a magnet sends the coded signal and power across the skin by radio frequency. Internally, a surgically placed **receiver-stimulator** decodes the signal and drives an **electrode array**, typically **12 to 22** electrode contacts, threaded through the **round window** into the **scala tympani** of the cochlea. The genius of the design is that it exploits the cochlea's own **tonotopy**: electrodes near the **base** of the array stimulate nerve fibers tuned to **high frequencies**, and electrodes deeper toward the **apex** stimulate **low-frequency** fibers. This is **place coding**: the processor splits incoming sound into frequency bands and routes each band to the electrode sitting at the matching tonotopic place, often using the **Greenwood map** to assign frequencies to positions.

The **processing strategy** determines how sound is converted to patterns of electrical pulses, and its evolution is the story of the implant's success. Early strategies struggled, but **Blake Wilson's continuous interleaved sampling (CIS)** in **1991** was a breakthrough: it stimulates electrodes **one at a time in rapid succession** (non-simultaneously) so that current from neighboring electrodes does not overlap and smear the place information, dramatically improving speech recognition. Later strategies such as **ACE (Advanced Combination Encoder)** and **n-of-m** select, on each cycle, only the few electrodes with the most energy, while **fine-structure** strategies attempt to convey temporal pitch cues. The result is that many implant users understand open-set speech, and some converse on the telephone, outcomes unimaginable before multichannel place coding. Implants are now offered to children as young as a few months under newborn-screening programs, because the developing auditory brain learns to interpret the electrical patterns best when stimulation begins early.

slides.title: Bone-conduction and implantable devices, and choosing among them
slides.body:
Between conventional hearing aids and cochlear implants lies a family of **bone-conduction** and **middle-ear** devices for patients whose problem is neither a simple amplifiable loss nor a totally dead cochlea. Matching the right technology to the right ear is a central clinical judgment.

**Bone-anchored hearing devices** (the original **BAHA**, or bone-anchored hearing aid, introduced commercially in the 1980s and built on **Per-Ingvar Branemark's** discovery of **osseointegration**, the same titanium-to-bone fusion that enabled dental implants) bypass the outer and middle ear by delivering sound as **vibration directly to the skull bone**, which conducts it to the cochlea. A titanium fixture is osseointegrated into the skull behind the ear, and an external sound processor snaps onto an abutment or couples through the skin magnetically. These devices are ideal for two situations the ordinary hearing aid cannot serve: a **conductive or mixed loss** where the ear canal or middle ear cannot transmit air-conducted sound (for example, **chronic draining ears**, **atresia** of the ear canal, or after radical mastoid surgery), and **single-sided deafness**, where the device picks up sound on the deaf side and routes it by bone conduction across the skull to the functioning opposite cochlea.

Other implantable options round out the toolkit. **Middle-ear implants** (such as the floating-mass transducer) attach a vibrating actuator directly to the **ossicular chain** to drive it mechanically, useful for some sensorineural losses or for patients who cannot tolerate ear-canal molds. **Auditory brainstem implants (ABIs)** place an electrode array on the **cochlear nucleus** itself, bypassing not only the cochlea but the entire auditory nerve; they are used when the eighth nerve is absent or destroyed, as in **neurofibromatosis type 2**, where bilateral vestibular schwannomas have been removed.

The decision tree is logical and follows directly from the pathology. If the cochlea has **usable residual hearing** and the outer/middle ear can carry sound, an **acoustic hearing aid** with WDRC is first-line. If there is a **conductive or mixed** loss that cannot be medically corrected, or **single-sided deafness**, a **bone-conduction** device routes sound around the blockage. If the cochlea is **profoundly damaged** so that amplification gives no useful speech understanding, a **cochlear implant** bypasses the hair cells and stimulates the nerve. And if the **auditory nerve itself** is gone, an **auditory brainstem implant** is the last resort. Increasingly, patients use **hybrid** or **bimodal** combinations, an implant in one ear with a hearing aid in the other, or **electric-acoustic stimulation (EAS)** that pairs a short electrode (preserving apical low-frequency acoustic hearing) with amplification in the same ear. The guiding principle, established across decades by **House**, **Clark**, **Wilson**, **Branemark**, and the audiologists who fit these devices, is to deliver sound by whatever route the surviving anatomy still allows.

question.question: Why do hearing aids use **wide-dynamic-range compression (WDRC)** rather than a single fixed gain?
options: Because fixed gain uses too much battery power.

Because sensorineural loss raises thresholds but often leaves loud sounds still uncomfortably loud (recruitment), shrinking the usable dynamic range; WDRC applies high gain to soft sounds and little gain to loud sounds, fitting the wide acoustic world into that narrow comfortable window.
Because compression makes all sounds equally loud regardless of input.
Because the microphone cannot handle loud inputs without compression.
question.explanation: Outer-hair-cell loss elevates thresholds yet often leaves loudness discomfort near normal, a phenomenon called recruitment, so the residual dynamic range may be only 30-40 dB instead of 120 dB. WDRC gives lots of gain to soft inputs and little to loud inputs, compressing the broad input range into the patient's comfortable range so soft sounds become audible without loud sounds becoming painful.

hints: Think about recruitment: thresholds rise but discomfort does not.
Compression means more gain for soft inputs, less for loud inputs.
slides.workedSolution: Sensorineural loss elevates thresholds while leaving loudness discomfort near normal (recruitment), so the comfortable range narrows to perhaps 30-40 dB. A single fixed gain would either leave soft sounds inaudible or make loud sounds painful. WDRC solves this by amplifying soft sounds heavily and loud sounds little, mapping the wide acoustic range into the patient's narrow residual dynamic range.

question.question: Choosing a device for single-sided deafness with a normal opposite ear.
question.prompt: A patient has a totally dead cochlea on the right (no usable hearing, profound) but completely normal hearing on the left. They struggle to hear people speaking on their right side and in noise. Considering why a cochlear implant might or might not be chosen and how a bone-anchored device handles single-sided deafness, reason about which technology routes sound from the dead side to the good cochlea and why.

question.question: How does a cochlear implant exploit cochlear **tonotopy** to convey pitch?
options: It vibrates the entire basilar membrane at once so the brain hears all frequencies.

It maps frequency bands to electrode position: basal electrodes stimulate high-frequency nerve fibers and apical electrodes stimulate low-frequency fibers, so the processor sends each frequency band to the electrode at the matching tonotopic place (place coding).
It amplifies sound acoustically before delivering it to the eardrum.
It plays louder pulses for higher pitches at a single electrode.
question.explanation: The electrode array lies along the tonotopically organized cochlea. Because basal regions naturally encode high frequencies and apical regions low frequencies, the processor filters sound into bands and routes each band to the electrode sitting at the corresponding place, often using the Greenwood map. Stimulating the right place evokes the corresponding pitch, this is place coding and is the foundation of multichannel implants.

hints: Recall which end of the cochlea encodes high versus low frequencies.
Each electrode sits at a tonotopic place and represents a frequency band.
slides.workedSolution: A cochlear implant uses place coding. The electrode array runs along the tonotopic cochlea, so basal electrodes stimulate high-frequency fibers and apical electrodes stimulate low-frequency fibers. The processor splits sound into bands (mapped by the Greenwood function) and stimulates the electrode at the place that naturally encodes that band, evoking the matching pitch.

question.question: A normal ear spans about **120 dB** of dynamic range, but a patient with recruitment has a usable range of only about **35 dB**. By approximately how many **dB** must the input dynamic range be compressed away to fit it into the patient's window? (Subtract.)
question.hint: Subtract the patient's usable range from the normal range: 120 minus 35.

question.question: Why early implantation matters for a deaf infant.
question.prompt: A baby is identified through newborn screening with profound bilateral sensorineural deafness and is a candidate for cochlear implantation. Drawing on the idea that the developing auditory brain learns to interpret the electrical place-coded patterns and on critical periods of auditory and language development, explain why audiologists push to implant early rather than waiting until the child is older, and what is at stake if implantation is delayed for years.
